---
title: "The example study"
---


The package ships a small synthetic study as a regular zotQDA exchange
pair, so every function that reads real exports has something realistic to
read in examples, tests and this documentation:

```python
frag = qdapy.read_fragments(qdapy.example("easyqda-fragments-demo.csv"))
hist = qdapy.read_history(qdapy.example("easyqda-history-demo.csv"))
```

The same two files ship byte-identically in the R twin
[qdaR](https://qdar.zotqda.org) (`qda_example("easyqda-fragments-demo.csv")`),
and a test in each package fails if the copies ever drift apart. Results
computed on them are therefore comparable across the two packages down to
the last digit, and both test suites freeze the coefficients below.

::: {.callout-important title="Reliability comes from the history, not the fragments"}
The fragments export is zotQDA's *last-state* table: one row per annotation
and code, with a single `codedBy` (last add wins). Where two coders coded the
same segment, that shape collapses — the fragments file keeps only the final
state and cannot tell you which coders agreed. Intercoder reliability is
therefore reconstructed from the **history**, the coding log with one row per
`add`/`remove` event, exactly as [qdaZ](https://qdaz.zotqda.org) computes it:

```python
codings = qdapy.codings(hist)               # replay the log to current state
matrix  = qdapy.units(codings, coder="user")
qdapy.agreement.agreement(matrix)
```

At the leaf codes this gives **α = 0.672** and **AC1 = 0.674**. Flattening the
paths to their top theme (`units(..., level=1)`) lifts it to **α = 0.897** and
**AC1 = 0.898**: coders who split over `Belastung/emotional` against
`Belastung/körperlich` still agree the segment is about `Belastung`. That
level effect is a statement about the code system, not the coders — and it is
the finding the example is built to show. The fragments file stays for the
corpus and last-state analyses (`code_counts()`, `code_matrix()`,
co-occurrence).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Synthetic, and saying so"}

Nothing here was ever said by anybody. The interviews, coders and
codings are generated from a fixed random seed, purely so that the
documentation can show real figures and the tests have stable
numbers. Any resemblance to actual studies is the point, not an
accident. But do not cite these numbers as findings.
:::

## What the study is

A fictitious interview study on workload in nursing: eight
semi-structured guide-based interviews, four from a ward (`Station-1` …
`Station-4`) and four from the administration (`Verwaltung-1` …
`Verwaltung-4`). The transcripts follow simple, smoothed rules with
speaker marks (`I:` interviewer, `B:` interviewee); the guide is handled
flexibly, and only the answers are coded. Two coders, `Anna` and
`Robert`, coded consensus segments (the same annotations, each with their
own code), following the three-phase method described in the
[zotQDA documentation](https://zotqda.org).

The code system has nine codes in three themes:

| Theme | Codes |
|---|---|
| Belastung | `Zeitdruck`, `emotional`, `körperlich` |
| Ressourcen | `Team`, `Autonomie`, `Anerkennung` |
| Bewältigung | `Humor`, `Distanz`, `Sport` |

## The structure built into it

Each property below exists so that one of the package's analyses has
something true to find:

* **The two settings have different theme profiles.** Burden codes and
  `Ressourcen/Team` dominate the ward, `Autonomie`, `Anerkennung` and
  `Distanz` the administration. This group difference is what
  `ca_map()` and `code_matrix()` show.
* **Burden and coping travel in pairs.** `emotional`↔`Humor`,
  `Zeitdruck`↔`Distanz`, `körperlich`↔`Sport` and `Team`↔`emotional`
  tend to be coded on the same passage. These co-occurrences are what
  `dendrogram()` and `mds()` recover.
* **The coders agree often, and disagree systematically.** `Robert` picks
  `Anna`'s code about 78 % of the time; when he differs, it is a
  within-theme neighbour or the partner code, never uniform noise.
  `confusion()` therefore returns a short, interpretable list.
* **Some cells are honest gaps.** `Robert` left about 7 % of the segments
  unrated (`alpha()` handles the gaps), and `Anna` occasionally coded a
  segment twice, so `agreement()["multi_set_aside"]` has something to
  count.
* **The history contains second thoughts.** Six codings were later
  removed; `timeline()` ignoring them is the documented behaviour, and
  `codings()` replays the removes so they never reach the reliability matrix.

Positions are present (`positionKind == "text"`), so `segments()` works —
but because the segments are consensus segments, both coders carry the
same boundaries, and unitizing measures on this file are trivially high.
Measuring unitizing for real needs each coder's *own* marks, which is a
different export.

## How it was generated

The two CSVs are a **genuine zotQDA export**, not a hand-written fixture.
`tool/gen-demo-study.js` in the zotQDA repository builds a native zotQDA
model of the study and drives the plugin's own exporters — the same code
that exports any real study — so the files carry exactly the shape and byte
layout a real export has. Run with `--distribute`, it also copies the CSVs
into this package (and into qdaR), which is what the cross-package identity
test relies on:

```bash
node tool/gen-demo-study.js --distribute
```

The design is fixed (seeded interviews and timestamps, no clock involved), so
the output is reproducible to the byte. The same study also ships as a native
loadable example inside the zotQDA plugin — a REFI-QDA project under
`examples/pflege-workload`, importable through the plugin's project import — so
you can open it in zotQDA itself, not only read its export here.

The old `script/make_demo_export.py` in this repository is retired: it now
prints this provenance and exits non-zero, so nobody regenerates the demo
through the former synthetic path.
